opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the single most common mistake is treating the first tweet like an abstract: "We study X in setting Y using method Z." Nobody cares yet. Most people will only ever read that first tweet, so it needs to stand alone and carry the whole payload.

My rough heuristic is that the first tweet should state the main claim, as concretely and punchily as you can while still being true. Not "we investigate the mechanisms behind refusal in language models," but something like "Refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction: remove it and the model stops refusing, add it and it refuses harmless requests." That's a claim someone can remember, repeat to a friend, and get excited or skeptical about. Either reaction is good.

A few other things I'd say. First, include a visual if you possibly can. A good figure in the first tweet does an enormous amount of work, and people scroll past walls of text. Ideally it's a figure someone can understand without reading the paper, which often means making a new one specifically for the thread rather than reusing figure 3.

Second, tell people why they should care. One clause on why this matters, whether it's "this suggests safety fine-tuning is shallow" or "this is a cheap tool you can use for X." People need a reason to click through.

Third, don't oversell. There's a real tension here: you want to be punchy, but you have a responsibility not to state things more confidently than your evidence supports. I'd rather lose some engagement than have a thousand people walk away believing something stronger than what I showed. Caveats can go later in the thread, but the headline itself shouldn't be false.

And finally, put the link and coauthors in, though often slightly later in the thread or at the end, because links in the first tweet can get down-ranked by the algorithm. Thank your collaborators, especially junior ones; it matters a lot for them.

More generally, I think researchers dramatically underinvest in communication. You spend six months on a paper and then an hour on the thread, but the thread is often what determines whether anyone actually reads the paper. It's worth spending real effort on it, and getting feedback from someone who wasn't involved in the project, because you are terrible at judging what's confusing about your own work.

r001.rationale: The response recommends leading with a concrete main claim, but does not say the first tweet need not demonstrate the writer’s expertise.

r002.rationale: It recommends putting the link later in the thread or at the end, noting that links in the first tweet can be down-ranked.

r003.rationale: It says an abstract-like first tweet fails to engage, but does not address presenting only a screenshot of the abstract, title, and authors.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the first tweet is the whole game, and most researchers get it badly wrong. The way I'd put it is: the first tweet is not a summary of your paper, it's an argument for why anyone should read tweet two.

So the mistake people make is they lead with the paper title, or "Excited to share our new work on X," or some fairly dense sentence that only makes sense if you've already read the abstract. And the problem is that on Twitter you're competing with everything else in someone's feed. They'll give you maybe two seconds. If the first tweet reads like an abstract, they just keep scrolling, and nothing else in the thread matters.

What I'd do instead is lead with the single most interesting thing. Not the method, not the framing, the result. What's the one claim that, if a smart person who works in a nearby area read it, they'd go "huh, wait, really?" That's your opener. Ideally it's concrete and a bit surprising. If there's a striking plot or a one-line finding, that goes in the first tweet, not tweet seven.

A few more things I think matter. Write it so someone with zero context can parse it. If you need jargon, you need less of it than you think. Make it specific rather than vague: "we found X does Y" beats "we study the relationship between X and Y." And it's totally fine to be a little bit bold about it, as long as the paper actually backs it up. The thread is where you add nuance and caveats. The first tweet is where you earn the right to be nuanced.

And honestly, the meta-point is that this is a skill, and you can practice it. Draft five versions of the first tweet, show them to a friend who hasn't read the paper, and ask which one makes them want to know more. That's a much better signal than what you think sounds impressive.

r001.rationale: The response recommends leading with an interesting result rather than method or framing, but does not say the first tweet need not demonstrate the writer’s expertise.

r002.rationale: The response gives no advice about whether to include the paper’s link in the first tweet.

r003.rationale: It says title-led or abstract-like text may cause readers to scroll, but does not address a screenshot showing the abstract, title, and authors.

astra-6.text: I think the first tweet should give people a reason to care. What’s the most interesting thing you found, and why does it matter? Don’t just say, “We’re excited to announce our new paper,” followed by the title. Tell me something that makes me want to read the next tweet. Ideally, even if I don’t read the rest of the thread, I’ve learned something from that first one.
